summary: Two review rounds checked the library guides claim by claim against the providers' own documentation. Round 1 (GitHub, Slack, Gmail): 52 items, 36 confirmed, 11 corrected, 5 unverifiable. Round 2 (all six library guides): 120 items, 74 confirmed, 39 corrected, 7 unverifiable. Every finding was applied to the guide; corrected claims show what the guide said before.
method: Independent reviewer agents (Claude), one per guide, read the guide JSON and checked items against primary sources with web search and fetch. Round 2 also separated three things in every guide: the wait required before any customer can connect through OAuth, optional listings (marketplaces, directories, certification), and limits after users connect. No accounts or apps were created; hands-on setup attempts remain a planned follow-up.

Its review takes up to 10 business days plus up to 10 weeks, after a 10-workspace/28-day prerequisite. The practical blocker for unlisted commercial apps is the 2025 rate limit: conversations.history/replies at 1 req/min

entries.after: Any Notion account works; you pick a development workspace when creating the connection (no separate developer account)
entries.evidence: https://developers.notion.com/guides/get-started/public-connections.md - required field "Connection name and development workspace"

lessons: The agent's biggest systematic error was treating optional marketplace reviews as OAuth approval. In round 2, three of six guides showed a required wait that was really an optional listing: Slack (0-84 days), HubSpot (1-10) and Notion (1-7); none of them needs a provider review before customers can connect. GitHub's summary also quoted the optional Marketplace timeline. Gmail went the other way: its real required wait is 42-70 days, because the scopes an agent needs are restricted. Microsoft has a short required wait (3-7 days, partner verification) and its real blocker is customer admin consent. The guide schema and the agent prompt now keep required waits, optional listings and post-connection limits apart.

The facts were mostly right; the verdicts were where the agent went wrong. Of 52 checked items, 36 were confirmed. But the GitHub and Slack verdicts named the wrong top blocker, and the Gmail wait was understated by about 2x. The verdict is the most-read part of a guide, so it is what we now review first.

The agent conflates optional and mandatory paths. Slack Marketplace review was presented as required, when public distribution needs no review. The product fix: guides now show both paths, and the 2025 rate limits explain why message-reading agents still end up on the Marketplace path.

Fine-grained classifications are easy to get wrong. The agent called gmail.readonly 'sensitive' and the CASA assessment optional; both are restricted/mandatory. Scope tables are now a review checkpoint.

Quote checking catches invented sources but not misapplied ones. A real Google quote about Workspace Marketplace review ('several days') was used as the OAuth verification timeline. It passed the verbatim check, so labels show where a quote came from, not whether the page answers the question.

Timelines are almost never in official docs. Google is the exception (its FAQ gives estimates). GitHub publishes none, and the agent's 2–6 weeks came from a community post and was presented as fact. Guides now label such figures as community-sourced.

Free-tier limits shaped the design: each Gemini model allows 20 requests per day. The pipeline rotates through models, uses a light model for identification, and records which model drafted each guide.
